of Commerce did not really want   to join the program. They did 
so only because they had to. So Dee Hock and his colleagues went to

by 1968, the system was on the verge of collapse. Nobody knew how much the banks would lose

America called a meeting of its bank licensees. Hock and others joined. There, the licensees

in the United Kingdom and other parts of Europe. Early devices used paper slips but

the evolution of bank cards and will   provide substantial benefits

just did not buy with credit, per cultural norms. Just like how Millennials today make "big 
purchases" on the "big screen" (i.e. a computer   rather than a phone), Americans in the 1970s

the money they already had in their accounts. And as for the member banks, the Entree 
card seemed like a winner too. It was not   only a natural extension to their profitable 
credit cards, it would also save them money. Paper checks for all their hundreds

and hurt revenue for certain payer banks. A few banks shunned the Entree card's signature 
debit method, believing that the aforementioned   PIN-based methods they already used for their 
ATMs worked better and were more secure. Finally and most importantly however, the 
banks saw fund transfer - and electronic fund   transfer in particular - as fundamental to their 
business. Sure, credit cards are profitable now,   but to the grumpy, old school bankers it 
was still one step away from the pawn shops. Real banking involved collecting and 
servicing deposit customers. And to   cede the future of their electronic funds 
transfer strategy to a third-party credit   card organization would be a generational fumble. In other words, the banks didn't hate the idea of   debit cards per se. They hated the 
idea of a debit card issued by NBI. When NBI changed their name to Visa in 
1976, the Entree card was rebranded to   the Visa Check Card. Despite the name change, 
less than a hundred banks adopted the product.   And by the end of the 1970s, the trade 
press was starting to call it a failure. ## The Two Cards So in the United States throughout the 
1980s, households typically had two cards. One of those was a credit card. By 1990, 
almost 65% of American payment cards offered   some form of revolving credit. You bought 
things with it using the signature method. But the other card that they almost 
always had was an ATM debit card - issued   to them by their bank for withdrawing 
money from an ATM via the PIN method. Over time, banks realized that customers 
wanted convenient access to their money.   So they put more ATMs in areas outside 
their branches. ATMs started to show   up at train stations, grocery stores, 
airports, convenience stores, and so on. Banks then realized that they can 
create and share networks of ATMs,   spreading out the upfront cost of 
installation. In the mid-1980s,   regional ATM networks like Yankee24 in New 
England or NYCE in New York started to grow. This was encouraged by a major 
ruling by the US Supreme Court   in 1985 that held that ATMs were not bank 
branches. This allowed these ATM networks   to expand across interstate lines into 
national networks like STAR or PULSE. In 1978, America had less than 10,000 
ATMs. By 1990, there were over 80,000 ATMs,   nearly 200 million debit cards and over 450 
million debit transactions conducted each month. ## A Plastic Menace
As consumers got more used to using ATMs, the networks realized that they can expand 
into a more critical space: the Point of Sale. This move began in earnest in the 1980s when 
a few supermarkets installed the terminals   necessary to handle PIN debit transactions. 
Doing so allowed the supermarkets to offer a   "cash back" option where the customer can do a 
purchase and cash withdrawal at the same time. Man, I remember people doing this in the 
line at the supermarket when I was a kid. This was a pretty compelling product, 
and it led the ATM networks to convert   into more generalized Electronic 
Funds Transfer or EFT networks   that can handle transactions at 
both the ATM and point-of-sale. So one day, Visa rolls out of bed and 
realizes that it has some serious competition.   The EFT networks' PIN debit cards 
debited customer accounts instantly,   were more secure fraud-wise, 
and inflicted no overdraft fees. Most importantly, their networks' 
pricing for facilitating transactions   were cheaper. Visa's debit card fees 
were structured like their credit cards:   As a percentage of the total purchase price. By contrast, the interchange fees for 
PIN debit transactions were - back   then - charged at a small fixed rate 
or even zero for some ATM networks. The fly in the ointment for the EFT networks 
however was that the merchants were not on board.   They did not have the necessary point-of-sale 
terminals to handle PIN debit transactions.   Part of the reason why was because the equipment   was expensive and the merchants 
were not being paid to do it. The movement of payments and networks 
and who gets paid is quite esoteric,   so I am simplifying. But the key conflict 
was that the merchants wanted to be paid   per-transaction interchange fees as 
compensation for installing the new   point-of-sale equipment - which can cost 
$1000+ each in a time when $1000 was a lot. Worse yet, early EFT networks were not 
interoperable, so the merchants had   to buy unique terminals for each card 
network they supported. And so there,   the EFT networks and their PIN 
debit systems were somewhat stymied. Visa and Mastercard would repeatedly say that 
debit cards do not compete with credit cards.   But the massive base of ATM debit cards, the 
growing regional EFT networks, and Visa's lack   of representation in the debit market - just 11% 
as late as 1994 - must have made them nervous. What if these regional networks consolidated 
into one widely used national debit card   network? What if merchants finally 
update their equipment to take PIN   debit payments? And what if PIN debit's 
lower interchange fees become the norm? ## Interlink and PLUS To address the rising competition from 
the ATM networks and their debit cards,   Visa pulled off two remarkable deals. In 1983, five of California's largest 
banks joined together to form a new   point-of-sale payments network called 
Interlink. Interlink let customers use   debit cards to make PIN debit purchases at 
participating retailers and restaurants. These five banks represented 50-60% of 
all the checking accounts in the state.   Of the eight million ATM debit cards in 
the state, they issued six million of   them. Interlink was an attempt to get those 
users to use debit cards for buying stuff. Somehow, Visa's US subsidiary won 
the contract to provide Interlink's   technical backend. Interlink grew into 
one of the country's largest POS debit   networks - turning the US West Coast into a 
debit card pioneer and helping Visa learn how   to process PIN debit transactions. 
They later acquired it in 1991. Visa also acquired their own ATM network. In 
1987, they paid $5 million for a 33% stake in   one of the national ATM networks, PLUS, along 
with an option to acquire the whole thing. With these two transactions, Visa assembled 
the technology and network for their own PIN   debit transactions. But a few voices 
argued that these two acquisitions   also allowed Visa to monopolize 
and control the debit market,   and suppress a superior alternative. What 
happened soon afterwards would fan those fears. ## Entree 2
Throughout the 1970s and 1980s, Visa and Mastercard had competed 
ferociously against each other. So it was somewhat of a surprise in 1987 when 
they announced that they were teaming up for a   point-of-sale debit card. The joint venture 
would be named - confusingly enough - the   Entree Card. Yes, the same name as that 
first debit card product in the 1970s. Mastercard had their own national 
ATM network, Cirrus. So Entree users   would be able to use ATMs in both the 
PLUS and Cirrus national ATM networks. 1.5 million of these second Entree 
cards were issued. But none of them   were used for making transactions 
because the retailers - obviously   fearing the power of a Visa-Mastercard 
combination - did not accept them. Then in 1989, 14 states launched an antitrust 
lawsuit against the joint venture. They also   wanted Visa and Mastercard to divest their 
interests in Cirrus and Plus as well as Interlink. They argued that Visa and Mastercard were 
trying to suppress competition by buying   their way into the networks handling debit 
card transactions. They also alleged that   Entree was an attempt to keep regional ATM 
networks from entering the debit card market. Visa and Mastercard argued briefly over this,   but a year later in 1990 they signed a 
consent agreement to terminate Entree.   However, they were allowed to keep their 
interests in Cirrus, Plus and Interlink. The anti-trust battle seemed to have somewhat 
spooked Visa against making further inroads   into the PIN debit market. For the next 
few years, their strategy and promotional   funds focused on building their standing in the 
signature debit market - starting with the banks. ## Take All Cards In the early 1990s, Visa embarked 
on a major effort to get banks   to add Visa branding to their ATM 
cards and accept signature debit. In 1991, the massive Chase Manhattan bank - 
predecessor of today's JP Morgan Chase - agreed,   converting 800,000 of their Money Cards 
to Visa-branded debit cards. Other large   banks soon followed, supercharging 
Visa's share of the debit card market. The reasoning for this was both 
cultural and economic. Culturally,   a new generation of bankers had taken 
over. The old school bankers who so   wanted to separate the credit cards and the 
deposits businesses were no longer around. Economically, Visa convinced the banks that they 
can earn more revenue from the percentage-based   interchange fees from signature debit 
transactions. Which at the time was 2%   of the total value of the purchase. The 
banks chose the better-paying option. Retailers hate this, of course. 
But their card agreements with   Visa or Mastercard require them to take all 
their cards, and that included debit cards. For certain plum customers, Visa adjusted 
the merchant fees to make it worth their   while. They did this for the supermarkets. 
Supermarkets hate how long it took for   customers to write out a check, but also hate 
credit card fees due to their low margins.   Visa lowered the debit card fees for 
supermarkets such that enough of them signed on. ## Signature or PIN? Debit card transactions continued to grow, 
hitting a total of 700 million in 1993. Even so, debit cards - PIN or signature 
- remained a small portion of the overall   payments landscape. In 1995, debit cards 
represented just about 2% of non-cash   payments at retail. Most people still 
preferred cash or ordinary paper checks. But this was about to change. Another 
selling point Visa had made to the   banks had been a promise to back the debit 
product with a massive marketing campaign. In the mid-1990s, Visa came through with a 
massive ad blitz. They really emphasized the   phrase "Check Card" - edging away from the phrase 
"debit", which sounded too similar to "debt". And directly repositioned the product 
as a convenient replacement for the   paper check. Paper checks still 
survive, but debit cards replaced   them for smaller purchases. The average 
debit card transaction was about $40. At the same time, merchant 
equipment got more widely adopted,   thanks to large reductions in price. By 1995,   swipe devices cost just $400, where a few 
years prior they cost well over $2,000. There was one final major trend. The emergence 
and rise of online e-commerce in the late 1990s   favored signature debit due to its flexibility 
for handling remote transactions. PIN-based debit,   more tailored to in-person purchases, 
never managed to get online the same way. Fueled by these three major trends and 
Visa's existing credit card infrastructure,   the Visa Check Card - and signature 
debit - consolidated the market. In 1994,   customers did 429 million PIN debit transactions   compared to 279 million signature debit 
transactions. PIN was strongly ahead. By 1999, the tables had turned, with 4 billion 
signature debit transactions, and just 2.9 billion   PIN debit. In 2003, 10.3 billion signature 
compared to 5.3 billion PIN transactions. ## Conclusion
This video has mostly focused on the US market. Assuming people care enough 
about this video topic,   I can do a separate one on Visa's dominance 
in Europe. They got that area in a lock too. There are arguments that Visa's 
actions in the debit card market   were anticompetitive. In this scenario, PIN debit   was winning out in the payments market. 
It was the technically superior option. Then big, bad Visa leveraged their 
titanic credit card monopoly - with   its unfair rules to honor every Visa 
card no matter what type - to enter   the debit card industry and crush 
that technically superior option. In 1996, Walmart and other merchants sued Visa 
and Mastercard, alleging this exact thing. In 2003, the two card companies 
settled just prior to going to   trial by paying several billion dollars and 
drastically cutting their debit card fees. Then in 2010, the Durbin Amendment in 
the Dodd-Frank Act capped the cost of a   debit card transaction, along with some other 
requirements. This largely ended any economic   argument that PIN had over signature debit, 
since they now both cost merchants the same. All the while, debit card transactions continue 
to grow alongside that of credit. Today,   Visa facilitates more debit payments than 
it does credit worldwide. Though they   probably make far more from its credit cards 
business, thanks to these debit card limits. The debit card market has changed greatly since 
the 1990s, but Visa remains dominant. In 2024,   the US Department of Justice sued Visa 
again over its debit card monopoly,   alleging that it is again using its size 
and importance to suppress competition and   generate massive margins. The outcome of that 
court battle remains uncertain. Stay tuned.

## 46. With Directed Self Assembly, the Chips Make Themselves (Kinda)

### Transcript:
At the 2024 SPIE Advanced Lithography 
and Patterning Symposium, Ann Kelleher,   a top Intel manufacturing executive, mentioned 
something called Directed Self-Assembly or DSA. In that presentation, she called DSA a 
key innovation for cost-effective scaling,   and said it had to be brought 
to High Volume Manufacturing. Intel later presented results of 
a DSA workflow that can "heal"   errors in EUV lithography - potentially 
cutting costs by a dramatic amount. But what is DSA? DSA has been around for 
over 30 years. It was once positioned to   be a replacement for photolithography, 
but now is seen as a complement to it. But will the fabs adopt it? In today’s video, 
a bottoms-up way to pattern the ever-shrinking   lines of our semiconductors: 
Directed Self Assembly, or DSA. ## Beginnings
Self-assembly is where materials spontaneously organize themselves into more 
complex shapes and structures. The self-assembling behavior is the result of 
information encoded in individual molecules and   atoms, plus natural, non-covalent 
forces like electrostatic forces,   van der Waals forces, or the hydrophobic effect. I am somehow reminded of economics, except it is 
not humans interacting with each other but very   small, nonsentient particles. The key thing is 
that the final arrangement is thermodynamically   favored. It minimizes the system's total 
free energy and is thus more stable. The purest form of self-assembly does 
not involve any external force, energy,   or applied field. But often times, we need to 
guide along the process to get what we want,   quickly and consistently. 
Ergo, directed self assembly. There are three generally accepted 
ways to do this direction. One,   we can design the building block materials' 
encoded behavior for the desired result. Two, we can prepare a template to 
direct the behavior. Self-assembly   requires the components to move 
freely, but we can use patterned   substrates to guide that movement like 
how traffic barriers redirect car flow. Three, we can apply a form of 
external energy to either induce,   guide or accelerate the interactions 
between the building blocks. This can   be an electromagnetic field, 
or simple thermal energy. DSA for semiconductor processes will utilize 
all three of these directing principles. ## Natural Self-Assembly
At first, this might sound super weird. Like as if your IKEA furniture spontaneously 
putting itself together inside its box. But self-assembly is a key organizing principle 
in the natural world. A nice example are these   compound molecules called amphiphiles. 
They have components with two natures,   one water-loving and one water-hating. In high enough concentrations in water, 
they will self-assemble into spherical or   cylindrical structures called "micelles". 
This is due to the hydrophobic effect. Micelles have their hydrophilic components facing 
outwards towards the water, while the hydrophobic   ones go inside. Note how the particles need to 
be allowed to move in relation with each other. This is the working principle behind how detergent 
or soap cleans you. The micelles encapsulate   oils and dirt inside their hydrophobic 
core, letting things to be washed away. Self-assembly is also abundant in biology   where it helps produce the lipid 
bilayers so essential to life. They also have applications 
to drug delivery systems,   since they can protect a drug 
from negative conditions. If we go to the geologic world, opals are 
beautiful end products of self-assembly.   They are colloidal crystals - formed 
from self-assembled arrays of what   we call colloidal particles packed 
together under moderate compression. In case you are wondering - as I was 
- "colloidal particles" is a fancy   name to describe micrometer-sized 
small objects suspended in a medium   like a solid or liquid. In the case of 
opals, those objects are silica spheres. ## Block Co-polymers
The most closely studied DSA building blocks are these unique compound molecules 
called Block co-polymers or BCPs. The phrase "co-polymer" describes a 
macromolecule made up of at least two different,   smaller molecules called monomers. The monomers 
are attached together like links in a chain. If the chainlink sequence is random - 
red, blue, blue, red, blue, red, red,   whatever - then this is what we call 
a random or statistical co-polymer. And if the chainlink sequence is consistently 
alternating - like as in blue, red, blue,   red - then the result is 
an alternating co-polymer. And now, if the chainlink sequence has 
repeating segments like blue-blue-blue   to red-red-red to blue-blue-blue, then each 
repeating segment becomes a block. When at   least two blocks are covalently bonded 
together, you get a Block co-polymer. Or shall I dare say, a block chain? The simplest possible BCP 
is a "diblock copolymer",   which is made from just two blocks. But 
there are more complicated BCPs out there,   with the blocks arranged in linear 
chains or star-like arrangements. ## Phase Separation BCPs are so special because 
of their internal tension. The block components are dissimilar. In fact, they 
literally repulse each other like oil and water. The force of that repulsion is 
measured using a metric called   the Flory-Huggins interaction 
parameter, which sounds like   a brand of diapers. It is represented 
by the Greek letter χ (chi or "kai"). The blocks' repulsion pushes them to 
minimize their direct interaction,   like as if they were two 
roommates who hate each other. However, the blocks' strong covalent 
bonds restrain their separation to only   a few nanometers. We can use this internal 
tension to produce complicated patterns. The process begins with spin-coating a   layer of BCP in a disordered or 
"dissembled" state onto a substrate. We kick off the self-assembly with a 
process called "annealing". With annealing,   we provide energy to the BCPs either 
through heat or chemical solvent means. The BCPs then try to separate 
the best way they can whilst   being chained together - eventually 
settling on an equilibrium structure. Going back to the roommates-who-hate-each-other 
metaphor - a familiar one for me - it is like   as if they split the room between themselves 
and now sit opposite across from each other. We call this process "microphase 
separation", and it is the heart of DSA. If done right, what results is an 
ordered structure of well-defined,   precise lines, spaces, and dots. Typically 
to complete the self-assembly process,   one of the blocks is removed, 
leaving behind the desired pattern. The resolution, or smallest possible 
size of the repeating final patterns,   is determined by the blocks' size and their 
aforementioned Flory-Huggins interaction   parameter (the diaper number). The higher 
the repulsion, the better the resolution. The contrast with traditional photolithography 
is fascinating. Photolithography is about taking   a block of material and carving away 
the unwanted portions. For that reason,   you can call it a "top-down" method. 
The pattern is imposed from above. DSA on the other hand builds up 
structures from the ground-up using   information programmed into each block. The 
pattern emerges out of the material itself. ## Block Copolymer Lithography BCPs were first demonstrated in 1995 at IBM,   and the goal was to outright replace 
the photolithography process itself. A team led by Mansky annealed a diblock copolymer, 
the simplest type of BCP, with just two blocks. The end result was an ordered pattern of tiny   spherical blobs arranged in 
a hexagonal grid. Pretty rad. Two years later in 1997, they tuned the 
process by adding what they called a "brush",   or what we now call a "neutral layer". 
During the self-assembly process,   BCP blocks might stick to a silicon 
substrate due to certain material biases. A neutral layer fixes this by acting 
kind like the ice for ice skaters,   allowing the components more freedom of movement. Mansky's clever trick was to 
use a random copolymer version   of the same block copolymer they were 
self-assembling. This allowed the team   to create 3D structures - layered 
stripes or tiny vertical cylinders. That same year, a team at Princeton led 
by Miri Park used diblock copolymers to   transfer patterned arrays of regularly spaced 
dots onto a substrate of silicon nitride. They then used a well-known 
etch technique called reactive   ion etching to pattern 20-nanometer 
wide dots into that substrate. This process flow is reminiscent 
of photolithography, which is why   they named this Block Copolymer Lithography. Such structures can be useful for certain 
nano-scale features for things like DRAM.   One major next-generation DRAM cell 
structure uses trench capacitors,   which are these deep trenches dug 
into the substrate. They argued that   self-assembly would work faster and cheaper 
than other methods like deep trench etching. Other suggestions include quantum dots or   the magnetic bits that high-density 
hard disk drives use to store data. IBM made other nano-sized objects for 
nonvolatile semiconductor memories. In 2003,   they used directed self-assembly to fabricate 
something called a nanocrystal memory cell. These are like traditional flash memory. But 
instead of using a single conventional film,   they use discrete, isolated particles called 
nanocrystals made using Chemical Vapor Deposition.   The IBM team used self-assembly to create a filter 
to standardize the size of the nanocrystals. In 2005, another IBM team used self-assembly 
to help produce the nanowire channels for a   nanowire transistor. Such wires 
were just 15 nanometers wide. ## Guiding Patterns This motivated some advocates 
in the 2000s to argue that   Directed self-assembly can be the future. In their argument, it can deliver 
resolution metrics on par with EUV,   but without the associated eye-popping 
financial and technological costs. However, questions remained. Defects were and 
remain a major problem. While it is true that   the DSAs want to achieve their thermodynamic 
ideal, they might not always get there,   which leaves defects. Reasons for 
such might include impure substrates,   external particles or an insufficient annealing. But the most significant question concerned a 
lack of top-down guidance. At a local level,   you can get these impressive, nanometer-sized 
structures. But at a macro level,   without guidance, the patterns lose their 
coherence. You get these patterns that look   like a fingerprint. Aesthetically 
pleasing, no doubt, but not useful. To deal with these issues, methods 
known as guiding patterns have   emerged. Two major guiding patterns 
are Chemoepitaxy and Graphoepitaxy. In Graphoepitaxy, we use traditional 
lithography to pre-pattern the substrate   with physical - or topographical 
- grooves. We then apply the BCP   layer between the grooves. Then we self-assemble 
to create tight lines or other structures. Chemoepitaxy runs on similar principles except 
that it uses chemical, rather than topographical,   patterns. We first apply a chemical and 
that chemical can either repel or attract   the blocks in the BCP during self-assembly. 
Almost like painting lines in a hallway. The Graphoepitaxy process seems to be 
simpler while also delivering tighter   lines, but Chemoepitaxy seems to offer 
fewer defects. In the readings I did,   there does not seem to be widespread 
consensus for one over the other. ## Density Enhancement By the mid-2000s, it had become clear however 
that only photolithography can meet all the   extreme demands - particularly with defectivity 
- that semiconductor manufacturers require. So researchers transitioned from developing DSA as   a lithography alternative to it being 
a complement via density enhancement. The idea is that the designs are getting ever 
tighter per Moore's Law. But photolithography   light dimensions hit 193 nanometers with ArF in 
the early 2000s and have stalled there ever since. But with EUV struggling then, fabs have 
been forced to adopt multi-patterning,   where they create multiple lower-density masks 
and superimpose those masks on top of one another. The simplest form of multi-patterning is 
double-patterning, but there are other,   more complicated process flows. Nonetheless, 
they are all very complex and require incredible   alignment. And mistakes can easily hurt yield. 
Fabs in general are loathe to multi-pattern. So the pitch is that DSA can be a fast and 
low-cost chemical method to cheaply improve   the resolution. Traditional lithography first 
lays down the guide patterns onto the substrate.   A layer of BCP is then spin-coated on top and 
annealed to produce a 2-3 times denser pattern. This gives you a very tight and 
dense regularly repeating pattern   that would otherwise require expensive 
multi-patterning at the cost of giving up   a little flexibility. But will fabs adopt 
it over other solutions on the market? ## 7-Nanometer Breakthrough? Starting in 2011, we started to get the first 
semiconductor equipment ecosystem consortiums,   trying to build new tools 
and flows that fabs can use. Notable members included IBM who did a lot of 
pioneering work, the Japanese equipment-maker   Tokyo Electron, the Belgian research institute 
IMEC and the French research institute CEA-Leti. The fervor for DSA seemed to 
crest in the early to mid-2010s,   when skepticism over EUV's 
effectiveness reached a nadir. In 2015, IMEC, Tokyo Electron, and Merck 
announced a potential breakthrough:   A DSA solution suitable for the 7-nanometer 
node. It produces an array of hexagonal   holes about 45 nanometers wide 
with relatively few defects. Advocates acknowledged that defect rates still 
needed to decline, but that DSA could cut   down on the need for one or two extra masks for 
producing contacts or vias. If that gets adopted,   then other processes can too - thus 
kick-starting an entire ecosystem. The fabs did seem to have given 
DSA a spin in their R&D labs,   but ended up going with multi-patterning 
for 7-nanometers. In a 2016 retrospective,   Mark Lapedus of Semiconductor 
Engineering reflects on the situation. He noted that DSA had not made fast enough 
progress in its biggest problem - high defect   rates, as well as roughness in the 
pattern. There were also outstanding   questions about how to integrate 
the process into existing flows. Then in 2013 and 2014, ASML made a major 
breakthrough in light source power. EUV   then started to make rapid progress 
towards high volume manufacturing.   The knowledge that EUV was on the way - and 
the billions of dollars already invested in   its ecosystem - sapped whatever momentum 
that DSA had for density enhancement. ## EUV Rectification EUV might have sapped DSA's first major coming 
out in the mid-2010s. But what EUV taketh away,   it also giveth. And it has given DSA a new 
reason for being: Stochastic variations. The dominant photoresist used today for EUV 
is the Chemically Amplified Resist, or CAR.   When an EUV photon hits the resist, it activates a 
chain reaction of chemicals that expand outwards. These are workhorses, but EUV lithography 
presents a special challenge for them.   They do not absorb EUV photons all that well, 
which sucks because dosages are already so low.   And being compounds, their absorption 
sensitivity is randomly distributed. This all means we get random variations that can 
cause roughness in the lines, especially at their   edges. These resolve into defects like unwanted 
line gaps or bridges between neighboring lines. Scaling down pattern sizes also creates new 
damages. As pitches reach the low 20-nanometer   range and beyond, we start experiencing 
pattern collapse, a major cause of defects. IMEC and Intel have proposed the use 
of DSA to potentially "rectify" these   delicate patterns. After EUV exposure, a layer 
of BCPs is then added on top. Self-assembly is   then activated with a 30 minute thermal 
annealing. The BCPs self-assemble over   the underlying guiding pattern, fixing the 
pattern's roughness and preventing defects. IMEC - working in concert with several 
South Korean universities - suggests that   this post-exposure rectification technique can 
possibly allow fabs to lower their EUV doses by up   to 60% for a 28 nanometer pitch design. Intel has 
presented similar results in their own work too. Smaller EUV doses mean less power and money spent. 
If it works, then that is music to fabs' ears.   Intel also sees DSA as being key to upcoming 
High-NA EUV machines, whose thin depth of   focuses mean thin resist layers that risk 
collapse. DSA can help heal those too. Pitch flexibility remains an issue. Defects too,   but Intel recently reported that they believe 
they can cut down the frequency of two major   defect categories by fine-tuning the dry etch 
and better filtering out external particles. ## Conclusion In a famous 1959 speech,   the physicist Richard Feynman shared a 
vision of billions of tiny factories. Miniature manufacturing systems capable of making 
items with previously-impossible precision. Feynman took it all the way 
down to the atomic level,   with nanomachines producing things atom by atom. Scientists like Eric Drexler have 
since argued the societal risks   associated with such "assemblers", 
and that they need to be regulated. DSA is pretty far away from those wild dreams. 
But the technology looks pretty compelling in   semiconductors. And as a crude bottoms up 
tech, it might be considered the first step   on a long path towards true nanomanufacturing 
like what Feynman called out many years ago.

## 47. Whatever Happened to China's Bandit Phones?

**Link:** https://youtube.com/watch?v=kgT6pTW8w44

### Transcript:
A phone with flashy bright 
lights and eight speakers. A phone with a massive battery. 
Falsely labeled of course. Olympics-branded phones. Cigarette pack phones. And of course, the "Motorpola". The 
mid-2000s saw the wild and wooly rise   of a bandit phone industry in 
the People's Republic of China. Fueled by incredible consumer 
demand for mobile phones,   a faulty regulatory system 
and a Taiwanese chipmaker. Whatever happened to those companies? Why 
couldn't they compete? In today's video,   the mid-2000s and the wave 
of Chinese bandit phones. ## Beginnings In 1992, four Chinese university students 
led by Xu Lihua started a company. They saw that Chinese people 
were rapidly adopting beepers. But all the existing beepers 
on the market were from abroad.   So their company would make Chinese 
beepers in China for other Chinese. Since they wanted their company to break out 
of its shell and soar, they named it Bird (波導). In case you are wondering. Beepers - or 
"pagers" if you swing that way - are an   older technology. Your typical beeper receives 
a message and then beeps you. You can then go   to a telephone to respond to the message. They 
got to be a bit of a status symbol in the 1990s. Bird raised money from a local town government 
and produced their first beepers in May 1993.   Shortages in Motorola beepers let Bird 
capture a small market niche. In 1998,   the peak of the beeper market, 
Bird sold 325,000 beepers. ## The Mirage In the late 1990s, beepers declined as 
consumers shifted to simple 2G mobile phones.   Today, you would call these feature phones. Bird's management sensed this shift as these 
phones gained popularity in Hong Kong and Korea   and decided to make their own mobile phones. But 
it wasn't as easy as just doing it. At that time,   the Chinese government required that every 
mobile phone maker be approved via a license. The licenses were highly limited. Between 1998 
and 2005, the Ministry licensed just 35 domestic   and 14 foreign phone manufacturers. 
And to protect domestic companies,   the foreign companies had to 
export 60% of their production. This created a bit of a market gap. People 
wanted or preferred a reputable Nokia phone,   but there was not enough supply. Certain 
unscrupulous Chinese companies realized   they can make a quick buck by imitating - 
i.e. counterfeiting - those reputable phones. Bird decided to try and build a brand of their 
own. They partnered with a state-owned company   for a legitimate mobile phone license. And 
to acquire the mobile phone technology,   Bird struck a deal with a French 
communications conglomerate called SAGEM. In September 1999, Bird launched the Mirage 
RC838 (幻影RC838). Made with a French mobile chip,   its name is derived from the French fighter

600+ million phones were sold that year. The year also saw a major decline

investments into phone chip development   led to significant margin declines 
in 2004. What can the company do? ## Lowering the Bar Now we return to Mainland China at 
a fascinating time in its history. In the 1990s, restructurings of state owned 
enterprises caused millions of Chinese to lose   their jobs. Many became migrant entrepreneurs, 
setting up small, informal workshops. These workshops had the will and desire to

Western companies like Texas Instruments had   little interest in catering their products 
to the needs of the local Chinese market. In 2004, the Chinese government recognized 
the folly of its strict licensing regime for   mobile phones, and replaced it with

introduced the "Turnkey Model". They designed   a highly integrated chipset with all the basic 
mobile phone features along with features like   image processing and MP3 file playback. 
The latter became particularly popular. They then bundled that chipset with a 
technical blueprint of a basic cellphone   called a reference design. The design 
included some hardware like a PCB and   schematic. The only thing left to do is to 
assemble it with a screen and plastic shell. And as for software, MTK offered a basic 
mobile phone operating system. Its core   was an embedded OS called Nucleus RTOS, 
first released in 1993. On top of that,   MTK layered on a special GUI called the 
MediaTek Advanced User Interface or MAUI. So what MediaTek was in effect doing 
was drastically lowering the barrier   for making a mobile phone by 
selling simple assembly kits. They were not the only ones doing this. 
There were the Chinese companies Spreadtrum   and Hi-Silicon. Texas Instruments and Qualcomm 
tried it too, though they failed. MTK led the   league. In one year, their share of Chinese 
mobile chipsets skyrocketed from 0 to 40%. ## Shanzhai These Chinese workshops - most 
of which were based in Shenzhen's   Huaqiangbei district (华强北) - did not make 
and sell the MTK reference design as is. That would not be a very smart business 
decision. There was no differentiation.   Instead, they engaged local designers 
and engineers to add special,   unique features on top of the reference 
design to make something brand new. Today we know many of these phones as 
"shanzhai" (山寨). It was said that these   early Shenzhen phone manufacturers were 
embarrassed to say their product was from   Shenzhen, so they instead printed "SZ". SZ 
became "Shanzhai", or so that story goes. But the term actually far predates the phones. 
In Hong Kong in the 1960s and 1970s, Shanzhai   factories were small family-owned workshops that 
subcontracted for garment and plastics factories. Their work was heavily manual: 
Assembling plastic flowers,   sewing garments, and trimming threads. 
And they worked out of either old   residential buildings or wooden huts in 
squatter areas on Hong Kong's hillsides. Shanzhai literally means "mountain fortress",   and it refers to a famous Ming Dynasty Chinese 
novel called "Water Margin". It's a long novel,   but the story follows over 100 bandits who hang 
out at a mountain and fight crime and corruption. It evokes the image of being on the outskirts 
- self-sufficient and rebelling against the   mainstream. So the English translation 
"bandit" probably makes sense here. And these phone workshops were then 
indeed breaking the law by putting   out phones without proper licenses 
and mobile network certification. MTK chairman Tsai has said in an interview 
that he prefers referring to them as "white   box" phones rather than "bandit", which 
carried a more negative connotation. ## Unique Shanzhai Phones It is true that many Shanzhai 
workshops copied the designs,   features, and even names of reputable companies. 
But they also gave us some truly unique pieces. There were bombastic phones with 
ultra-flashy LED lights or very   loud speakers. These were popular with 
farmers working in loud environments. As   well as youths in the rural areas, where 
30-50% of these phones were sold to. Shanzhai phones pioneered multi-SIM 
slots - capable of holding two,   three or even four SIM cards - long 
before it went mainstream. Using this,   users can easily switch between different 
carrier plans for better coverage or cost. There was a solar powered mobile phone,   presumably made for those living 
without easy access to electricity. There was a phone with a huge telephoto 
lens attached to its digital camera.   This was apparently made to cater to 
either photography enthusiasts or perverts. With an MTK chipset, a workshop can 
take a phone concept from paper to   reality in just about 2-3 months. Rough 
estimates at the time found that two to   three new feature phones were being 
released into the market each day. The fast time-to-market meant that workshops 
can ride trending topics for a quick buck.   In the run-up to the 2008 Beijing Olympics, 
they made phones with designs inspired   by the National Aquatics Center or the 
Bird's Nest stadium or the mascot Fuwa. A superfun phone was the "Buddha 
light phone" (佛光機), which targeted   Chinese Buddhists with design 
elements inspired by Buddhist art,   as well as a hardware slot to attach 
golden Buddhist charms against evil. Another favorite is the "cigarette pack" 
feature phone. Since cigarettes were/are   a regular part of Chinese business 
culture, the phone was apparently   popular amongst businessmen who found 
it a novel conversation starter. Nowadays, Chinese internet users nostalgically 
celebrate these knock-offs for their cheapness,   creative tweaks, and generally wild nature. It 
was a great way to express your individuality. It was a true Cambrian Explosion of 
creativity. I highly recommend that you   check out this website called "SHANZHAI 
ARCHEOLOGY (2015-2018)" by DISNOVATION.   Wonderful art piece that elicits the 
nostalgia of many Mainland Chinese. ## Bird Falls Bird, the Chinese mobile phone pioneer, 
quickly found itself in real trouble. They had been big during the older licensing 
regime, but now they were caught in the middle.   Below them, the Shanzhai phones 
were overwhelmingly cheap while   also sporting premium features like 
MP3 playback and dual camera support. And above them, the foreign 
brands’ phones like Nokia, Samsung,   and Motorola had their own superior technology, 
software, financial resources and user experience. Bird - with its big marketing budgets 
- could not afford to develop their   own technology. R&D never exceeded 5% of revenue.   What technology they did have was limited because 
it came through their foreign partner, SAGEM. Back in 2003, Bird tiptoed into automobile 
manufacturing. Bizarre. But then in 2006 they   doubled down in an attempt to diversify. 
This not only failed as spectacularly as   you might imagine it would - losses totaled 
nearly 600 million RMB - but also distracted   the company from its imploding phones 
business. I call it the anti-Xiaomi. So after sustaining brutal losses, Bird 
switched to real estate development,   which I reckon is like retirement for 
Chinese companies: Easy money with   little work. So far as I can tell, they are 
still around, but just a shell of themselves. ## Shanzhai Godmother In one way, China had something special - a 
thriving, high-energy tech manufacturing industry. The issue, however, was that much of that 
vitality depended on being outside of Mainland   China's regulated phone ecosystem. And many 
Shanzhai businesses argued that the marketing,   technology and regulatory burdens 
made it uncompetitive to go “legit”. Take the lesson of the greatest 
company of the bandit phone era:   K-touch, owned and operated by the ambitious 
"Shanzhai Godmother", Rong Xiuli (榮秀麗). Rong was born in 1963 in a rural village in 
Henan, and was often remembered as tomboyish   and stubborn. In university, she studied 
internal combustion engines and first worked   at a public research institute before 
quitting in 1993 to go into business. She first joined a mobile phone 
sales agent company reselling   Samsung and Dopod phones into China. 
In 1995, she bought out her boss and   his unsold inventory and grew the 
company into a powerful distributor. Then in 2002, she took all her savings and 
founded Beijing Tianyu (天语), or K-Touch,   with the goal of making their own phones. At the 
start, the company struggled to do that - invested   eight months and over 80 million RMB into 
R&D. It put them on the verge of bankruptcy. Then in 2005, she discovered MediaTek and 
its turnkey model. MTK dispatched a team to   deal with any technical issues and got things 
off and running. K-Touch acquired a Chinese   phone license and contracted OEMs to produce 
dozens of lines of cheap, low-cost phones. ## Going Big Rong used the familiar sales 
agent model to sell phones. In this arrangement, K-Touch first sold the 
phones in bulk to individual sales agents,   collecting cash up front. The sales agents are   then free to resell their stock 
to customers however they choose. Rong apparently liked this model because 
it was less restricting on the agents.   Being an auntie from Henan, she 
enjoyed the art of the haggle,   telling the Chinese broadcaster 
CCTV in a rare interview: > A handset distributor sells other 
people's products. But the marketing   model and the prices are decided by the 
big foreign players such as Samsung and   the like. The agents don't have a say 
at all, so selling is not much fun In 2006, K-Touch sold 10 million phones,   mostly to rural youths who liked the phones' 
slick looks and good build quality. In 2007,   sales exploded to 17 million and 10% 
market share. And then in 2008, 24 million. But problems were on the horizon. In 2008,   the Chinese government abolished the 
mobile phone licensing system altogether.   Now any Chinese company can go into the industry 
and it unleashed a flood of brand new entrants. Rong knew what all this competition meant, 
and decided that the way to beat them was to   "go legit". In other words, the Shanzhai 
Godmother wanted to climb up into the   middle to high ends of the market alongside 
Nokia, Samsung and the other foreign brands. In 2008, K-Touch released the K-Touch 
C800, the world's first 8-megapixel   cameraphone with 3x optical zoom. 
A legitimately well-made product,   it was Mainland China's first domestic phone 
to be priced at over 2,000 RMB or $287. She sought out foreign investors to add 
legitimacy to her efforts. In May 2008,   an American private equity fund 
called Warburg Pincus invested   $75 million for a 10% stake. This made Rong 
one of China's richest tech entrepreneurs,   with an estimated fortune of 4.2 
billion RMB or ~$600 million USD. Rong told the media that her goal was to make 
K-Touch the "Nokia of China". A term that I   think was loaded with irony considering what 
was happening to Nokia itself at the time. ## The Wrong Choice The C800 hardware was quite good, but the software 
ran the Windows Mobile 6.0 operating system. Ew. At a time when the iPhone's popularity 
and groundbreaking nature was becoming   rapidly obvious, this was not attractive. 
MediaTek realized it had to respond to   the iPhone somehow. And unfortunately 
they backed the wrong horse, at first. In 2010, MTK chose to partner with Microsoft. 
They seemed to have thought that Windows   Mobile was the "safer" choice and that 
the Windows product was more "mature". Unfortunately, Windows Mobile was not it. Android 
was, for reasons that I will get to in a future   video. Powered by Qualcomm chips, Android 
blew away the MTK and Windows Mobile pairing. MTK's revenues dipped in 2011 - partially 
as a result of business lost to the growing   Google-Android-Qualcomm juggernaut. Frantic, 
they brought out new chips like the MT6575   and MT6577 to support Android 4.0 in early 
2012, which restored MTK to growth and beyond. However, the lost years were more than enough 
to cripple many of MTK's customers like   K-Touch. MTK's decision meant that they had 
no choice but to first adopt Windows Mobile.   But K-Touch phones like the E61, E68, and 
E608 failed to match up against Android. K-Touch did a phone with Android that is 
mostly forgotten, but then bizarrely pivoted   to Alibaba's cloud-based Linux OS Aliyun 
(阿里云OS) powered by an Nvidia Tegra GPU. This decision was apparently driven by the 
belief that HTML5 apps will eventually overtake   native apps. However the user experience was 
apparently not quite there and sales of Aliyun   phones like the K-Touch W700 flopped - with 
70,000 units sold versus a million expected. K-Touch's last relevant phone was in 2012. 
They then tried to pivot to e-commerce before   undergoing significant layoffs, before fading 
into obscurity. Today their headlining products   are "elderly phones" with big buttons, 
large fonts, and long battery life. ## The Fall of Shanzhai The rest of the Shanzhai phone 
industry was by then fading away too. In late 2010, the Guangdong provincial 
government started cracking down on the   illegal aspects of the Shanzhai business 
model - IP infringement, counterfeits, etc. Meanwhile, new distribution models emerged. Most   notably the telecom operator-driven 
sales model, where telecoms subsidize   a cheap but reputable smartphone to 
lock a customer into a long contract. Coolpad and ZTE were examples of low to 
mid range smartphone brands that became   successful and widespread via this method. The 
telecoms had widespread distribution into the   lower tier cities and the rural areas. And their 
subsidies leveled the playing field price-wise. And of course, in 2011 Xiaomi released their 
revolutionary phone Xiaomi Mi 1. They offered   a well-regarded flavor of Android and a powerful 
Qualcomm chip at an incredible price - 1999 RMB. Why buy a shady, unsupported phone 
when these far better options exist?   The Shanzhai phone industry lost its reason 
for existence - the super cheap prices and   rural accessibility - and faded away. A 
few remaining companies like Transsion   fled overseas to places like Africa. 
Where they are now quite successful. ## Conclusion If you recall correctly, two major 
suppliers - Intel in hardware and   Microsoft in software - captured 
all the value in the PC supply   chain. Leaving nothing for the PC 
assemblers and other manufacturers. A similar thing happened in the Chinese 
shanzhai phone industry in the mid-2000s.   MediaTek's fully integrated chips, R&D 
spend, and turnkey model helped it capture   virtually all the value in that industry, 
leaving just scraps for the handset makers. And those handset makers had no way out of 
it. They did not yet have the talent base   to make a modern chipset, nor did they 
have the profits to fund the R&D anyway. So while we look back at it now with a bit 
of nostalgia, in reality the Shanzhai were   dysfunctional, desperate companies that only can 
exist because they didn't follow the law, cut all   sorts of corners in a rush to market, and skipped 
all kinds of essential long term things like   R&D. And in the evolutionary tree of Chinese phone 
history, they ultimately constituted a dead end.

fraudsters trying to pass off wheat   imports as being locally grown to get free money. ## The Wheat Boom As expected, these policies supercharged 
the Saudi agricultural sector. In 1980, the Saudis had about 
609 hectares of cultivated land,   which was about a small 19% 
increase compared to 5 years prior. By 1985, the amount of cultivated 
land had leapt to 946 hectares. Over the same time frame, vegetable production 
nearly doubled from 756,000 tons to 1.4 million   tons. Alfalfa or green fodder production 
grew four-fold to 2.1 million tons. But those categories paled next 
to the cereals. And within that,   wheat. Cereals production grew from 268,000 tons 
in 1980 to 2.2 million tons in 1985. Wheat was   over half of that. A huge leap from 1975, when 
Saudi Arabia produced just 3,000 tons of wheat. In 1984, the Saudis reached wheat 
self-sufficiency, even producing a   small surplus. That year, Saudi Arabia gave 
Bangladesh 50,000 tons of wheat as food aid. A year later, they started selling 
wheat to neighboring Gulf countries.   The Saudi King talked about 
being the bread basket of   the Gulf - exporting wheat to Europe 
and the People's Republic of China. In 1983, the US Secretary 
of Agriculture at the time,   John Block, remarked that he thought the program 
was crazy - implying that it was a waste of money. The remarks drew a response from the Saudi King 
himself, who vowed to refute such allegations.   The government said it was "thrilling story of 
real success". And I suppose Block was eventually   shushed down by the US Secretary of Commerce, who 
was loving all the US farming machinery exports. ## Crazy? There are a few reasons to agree 
with Secretary Block’s assessment. First, the whole program was costing a lot of 
money. Contemporary estimates of total investment   from 1980 to 1984 - when wheat self-sufficiency 
was reached - was over $18 billion. That is a lot of money for an industry 
that's just 2% of Saudi Arabia’s non-oil   GDP. It doesn't make much financial sense to 
spend $5 on grain that otherwise costs $1 or   so to import. Even with the oil industry 
throwing off some $300 billion a year. Second, humans eat more than just wheat. In 
1981, Saudi Arabia imported 90% of its food:   $1.4 billion worth of animals including 
6 million heads of goats and sheep,   12.1 million chickens and 252 million eggs; And $2.1 billion worth of vegetable 
products including 685,000 tons of corn,   427,000 tons of rice, and 2.3 million tons of 
barley. What progress were they making on that? In 1984, the Saudi government 
told reporters that they were   almost halfway self-sufficient 
in chickens, milk and eggs. Over the rest of the decade, the Saudi 
chicken industry grew from 140 million   birds and 1.8 billion eggs in 1984 to 270 
million birds and 2 billion eggs by 1990.   Despite this surge in domestic production,   even faster growth in chicken consumption meant 
that the country still had to rely on imports. And in the case of other 
meats like sheep and cattle,   the traditional farms raising 
those animals relied on older,   unoptimized methods. Such methods struggled 
to scale even with financial incentives. Even if they succeed in those 
other foods, analysts pointed   out that all that had been done was to 
shift the country's import dependences   from said food products to food inputs 
like fertilizers, seeds, and equipment. Third, the policy was not helping to 
create a large indigenous class of   productive farmers. Reporters at the 
time noted that many of the booming   wheat farms were owned by foreigners. Where 
was the technology and expertise transfer? ## The Water Cost But to me, the most significant cost 
was the use of groundwater. The scale   of water being withdrawn to irrigate 
the wheat fields was staggering. Between 1980 and 1984, Saudi farmers installed 
over 12,000 of these center pivot irrigation   systems - mechanized sprinkler systems where 
crops are irrigated around a center pivot point. It gives you these distinctive looking garden 
circles. Each center pivot covers 200 acres   of crops, and during operation can use 
up to 1,200 gallons of water a minute. In 1980, Saudi Arabia used 1.8 billion 
cubic meters of water for agriculture,   80% of total demand. Five years later, 
agricultural water use had exploded to   7.4 billion cubic meters, or 
about 1.95 trillion gallons. And where did all of this water come from? Some of 
it was renewable desalinated seawater, the usage   of which expanded from 63 million cubic meters to 
400 million cubic meters between 1980 and 1985. But most of the water used for the country's wheat 
self-sufficiency initiative - over 70% - came out   of the ground. 10,000 year old groundwater 
that is classified as "non-renewable". And yet despite the water usage - and 
the fact that self sufficiency in wheat   had been achieved - the guaranteed wheat 
purchasing policies continued throughout   the 1980s. To the Saudis, wheat 
was a strategic commodity - maybe   just as important as oil. With it they 
nullified any threat of a wheat embargo. And then there was the politics. By the late 
1980s, the wheat subsidy program had turned   into a government wealth transfer to the 
rich. Half of wheat production came from   1% of the country's farmers. In other 
words, the biggest and richest farmers,   and they lobbied hard against any potential 
threat to their position as the top crop. ## The 1990s This finally changed in the 
1990s, which saw a retracing   of some of the Saudi agricultural policies. This was for several reasons. The concerns 
about water sustainability. And oil prices   no longer being as high as they used 
to be, straining government finances. And of course, you had the outbreak 
of the First Gulf War in 1990. Saudi   Arabia played a large financial role 
in that conflict, putting billions   of dollars behind the coalition as 
well as into humanitarian efforts. By then, agricultural water demand had surged to 
new heights. In 1991, Saudi farms used 23 billion   cubic meters of water. That year, the Saudi oil 
industry pumped 470 million cubic meters of crude.   In other words, in 1991 the Saudis pumped fifty 
times more water than oil out of the ground. And nearly half of all that 
water was being used to grow   wheat. A close second were fodder 
crops like alfalfa for livestock. Moreover, there was evidence that the 
Five-Year Plans badly underestimated   how much water the farms would 
use - incorrectly estimating how   much cultivated land there was as 
well as the per-acre water demand. ## Scaling Down In 1994, the Saudi government 
cut the guaranteed price it   paid for wheat from 2,000 Saudi 
Riyals per ton to 1,500 Riyals. They also delayed payment 
delivery by up to three years,   which caused a lot of smaller farms to drop out. The government also indirectly reset the price 
of water by tripling the price of diesel fuel,   which is used to power the water pumps. These changes in policy had immediate impact 
on the wheat production totals. In 1992,   Saudi Arabia produced 4.1 million 
tons of wheat, the peak wheat feat. Two years later, that fell to 2.6 million 
tons of wheat. The year after that, 1995,   production crashed nearly 40% to 1.6 million tons. With consumption at 1.9 million tons, Saudi 
Arabia was no longer self-sufficient in wheat   for the first time since 1984. This 
remained the case for another decade,   wheat production hovering at 
just about 80-90% of consumption. Then in 2008, the government started 
phasing out the wheat subsidy programs.   The phase-out lasted several years 
- was finally completed in 2015.   That year, the country extracted 17 billion 
cubic meters of nonrenewable groundwater. The country continues to grow other foods 
domestically like dates, barley, animal fodder,   and vegetables. And while they are trying more 
water-efficient methods like drip irrigation,   an unsustainable amount of water 
is still being pulled up. In 2020,   9.7 billion cubic meters of 
nonrenewable groundwater was pulled. ## Sinking Lands In 1984, the Saudis inventoried 
their largest groundwater aquifers. They estimated that the aquifers had about 
500 billion cubic meters of water or about   132 trillion gallons of water. If we take 
those estimates at face value - though   we probably shouldn't - then about 
half of that was consumed by 1996. When reservoirs get depleted, 
a few things might happen.   The water table either falls further 
underground, forcing people to drill   their wells even deeper. Or the water that 
does come up is saltier, requiring filtering. There is also land subsidence. Removing 
the water causes the land to sink down   and compact together more tightly to fill the 
void. This subsidence highly depends on local   conditions, but can destabilize subsurface 
cavities, creating fissures and sinkholes. In the end, the most significant thing 
is that the groundwater cannot be used   for some other use. Industrial. Residential. 
With even the largest desalination plants in   the world unable to provide enough water for the 
urban population, the well water might be better   off being used by the people, rather than being 
fed to plants that can otherwise be imported. ## Conclusion Few can disagree that nations should strive 
for some form of food self-sufficiency. The reasons for this are starkly 
obvious. The 2022 outbreak of war   in Ukraine disrupted wheat exports. And so 
Saudi Arabia has restarted their government   purchasing programs. Production still 
trails consumption, but the trend is up. Yet it can be hard to balance 
these demands with the realities   of a country's limited natural resources. 
And the reality is that much of the water   pumped up from the ground - like 
its oil - will never come back. In the end, what probably works best is something 
in the middle. More desalination preferably   powered by solar. More water recycling and 
conservation. In the end, that is probably what   closes the gap. What happened with the first Saudi 
self-sufficiency program should not happen again.
