Satellite Business Systems or SBS. SBS wanted   to put up a fleet of satellites to provide 
businesses with communications services. AT&T's fear was that satellite would 
let IBM make an end-run around its   billion-dollar copper network, turning it into 
a stranded asset. All these developments meant   that - in AT&T’s eyes - they had no 
real choice but to go into computers. ## IBM vs. AT&T In this battle of the giants, IBM's position in 
computers and data processing seemed unassailable. Having solidly captured the market in the 
mid-1960s with their breakthrough System   360 computers, IBM still held 65% of the 
mainframe industry over twenty years later. A few years ago in the late 1970s, there was 
the public perception that IBM had gotten too   slow and bureaucratic to compete in new spaces 
like microcomputers. But the amazing success of   the IBM PC dispelled that, and in 1982 IBM 
seemed more invincible than ever before. The guys at AT&T knew they faced a 
formidable opponent, and that people   doubted that they can handle the competition 
after 30+ years in a monopoly environment.   But they argued that people should not 
discount their chances right off the bat. With the PC ascendant, retailers and partners were 
starting to be concerned that the microcomputer   ecosystem would be consolidated and 
controlled by one company: IBM. AT&T   wanted to make it clear to those concerned 
that they would be a reliable alternative. And they had technical chops too. Through 
Bell Labs, they created many of the core   technologies behind modern computers like 
the iconic transistor. And for decades,   they produced their own computers and 
terminals for managing telephone records. Through Western Electric, AT&T even made 
their own semiconductors. As it became clear   that they were going to make commercial 
computers, AT&T had Bell Labs design and   Western Electric fab a new state-of-the-art 
CPU: The 32-bit WE32000 or BELLMAC-32. And seemingly most importantly, AT&T 
owned a very special asset. AT&T had UNIX. ## UNIX UNIX will forever stand as a monumental 
landmark in computing history. It was first developed inside Bell Labs 
by Ken Thompson and Dennis Ritchie as   a simpler alternative to an earlier, failed 
time-sharing computer project called Multics. UNIX bundled several helpful features 
into a single system. Like for example,   a standardized, hierarchical file system that   abstracted away storage complexity 
by turning everything into a file. A command line interface that allowed 
the user to easily interact with the   system. If you know the right commands of course. A set of small, single-purpose programs like 
"ls" and "grep". The outputs of which can be   chained together using something called 
"pipes" to accomplish more complex tasks. Then in 1973, Thompson and Ritchie rewrote the 
UNIX kernel in a new, higher-level programming   language called C. C made the operating system 
portable - able to run on cheap, modest hardware. You can take all the software you have 
and drop it into another UNIX computer. ## The Spread of UNIX Perhaps more important than 
UNIX's technical features   was its unique economic and cultural situation. In 1956, AT&T struck a Consent 
Agreement with the United States   government that let them keep their 
manufacturing arm Western Electric.   As part of the decree, AT&T agreed to stick 
to its core business of phone service. AT&T and the Bell System used UNIX 
extensively inside the company.   However because of the Consent 
Decree, AT&T could not sell this   pretty functional tool to traditional 
commercial customers like businesses. So Western Electric licensed UNIX to 
universities for basically nothing, about   $250. But they offered nothing other than the 
code. Requests for new features? Bug reports? Nah. So grad students in universities like UC Berkeley 
modified the code, adding popular features like   networking. Some of these "remixes" like BSD UNIX 
became quite popular amongst certain circles. Starting in 1982, AT&T started cleaning 
up and consolidating the many UNIX   variants it then had under its control - 
so excluding Berkeley's BSD or Microsoft's   XENIX - so that they can create a single 
"canonical" UNIX for commercial clients. In 1982, they released UNIX System III 
- which combined a mix of internal UNIX   flavors like Writer's Workbench and Programmer's 
Workbench. Still intended for internal use,   it was nevertheless an important 
preparatory step for commercialization. Then in January 1983 at UniForum, they announced 
UNIX System V - the first commercial version   of UNIX - with improved file utilities 
and standardized libraries. AT&T started   licensing System V to computer makers with 
the goal of making it an industry standard. Though it should be important to 
note that System V still lacked   certain popular tools that non-AT&T UNIX 
variants had. Like for example the shell,   which is a command-line interface for 
inputting programs and communicating   with the OS. Many users seemed to prefer 
BSD's Berkeley Shell over System V's shell. ## UNIX's Role AT&T's strategy was to be the 
integrated all-in-one provider of   everything touching data from networks 
to computers to phones to software. Their market entrance strategy involved 30 
products across a range of verticals. For   businesses, AT&T would sell its first digital PBX, 
the Dimension System 85. From there, they will   expand into office automation by introducing 
a series of tools integrated with the PBX. For residential, AT&T will attempt 
to put a bunch of equipment into   households. A small personal computer or 
"home terminal" device bundled along with   their telephone - possibly connected 
to other computers in the area. The idea is that at some point, 
people at home or work will want   to communicate with others using their 
computer. And the computer they use the   most will eventually dictate the 
communications services they get. UNIX would be the sinew tying all these machines 
together. Its portability and nonproprietary   "open" nature would let UNIX programs communicate 
with each other and work in parallel with ease. John Knapp, publisher of the UNIX World magazine, 
extolled the possibilities in an 1984 editorial. In it, he positioned IBM (and 
Apple) as proliferating proprietary,   non-compatible standards. Standards that 
lead consumers down a road of wasteful   planned obsolescence. AT&T with UNIX on the 
other hand offered a different path, saying: > AT&T et al. have discovered in the Unix system   the great equalizer. By offering a relatively 
hardware-independent software environment,   the good guys are loosening 
the shackles of forced loyalty ## Making the Move To execute on its new mission, AT&T did 
an unusual number of outside partnerships. In late 1983, AT&T announced that they had paid   $260 million for a 25% stake in Olivetti, 
the Italian computer maker. Olivetti also   agreed to make and supply AT&T with a 
personal computer to sell into the US. A month later, AT&T announced 
that it signed a second deal   with an American computer-maker 
called Convergent Technologies. Convergent was a small OEM computer maker 
founded by former Intel and Xerox PARC employees,   producing hardware for other companies like 
Burroughs and NCR to sell under their own names. Considering we are talking about AT&T, it 
feels weird to see all these partnerships.   Almost like as if, after so many years of 
being restricted in who they can work with,   they went overboard in the other direction. Anyway. In March 1984, AT&T made the announcement 
everyone was waiting for. That they were   taking the giant IBM head-on and that they were 
committed. James Olsen, AT&T's vice-chairman said: > We intend to play in the 
market, and play in it well. ## Challenges Outside observers pointed out two major 
questions about AT&T's computer strategy. First, AT&T was at a substantial 
sales disadvantage against IBM.   They didn't start with nothing - AT&T 
had 900 directly-owned phone stores,   6,000 third-party outlets, 
and its own sales force. But AT&T had not seriously competed in a 
competitive market for a generation. And   IBM's sales and marketing savvy was world 
famous. There will have to be a transition. Dave Scott, VP of systems development at a 
company called Logisticon, said about AT&T: > "If you look at AT&T’s marketing policy for 
UNIX, you’ll see that it is not enlightened   about how to sell to Original Equipment 
Manufacturers and Value Added Retailers ... > AT&T’s marketing stance contrasts sharply with 
that of IBM, DEC and HP. These manufacturers   understand how to structure OEM pricing, 
that they need to be flexible in their   licensing policies and that different customers 
desire different levels of technical support" Second, UNIX was strong in educational 
and science applications, but lacked a   presence in useful applications for 
small businesses. Jack Campbell,   president of the UNIX workstation 
maker Fortune Systems, said: > "You look at an IBM machine with 
its communications packages, office   automation software and accounting programs, and 
compare it to what AT&T is offering: nothing" AT&T knew this, of course. And it seemed 
promising to outsiders that they reached   out to third parties to try and shore 
up this weakness. Another major deal   struck in early 1984 alongside the ones 
with Olivetti and Convergent was with   the software company Digital Research 
Inc, to produce a System V library. Digital Research Inc is most well known as 
being founded by Gary Kildall - creator of   the CP/M operating system that dominated the 
computer world before the ascension of DOS. ## Meet the Computers In June 1984, at the popular Comdex trade show 
held in the Los Angeles Convention Center,   AT&T announced the first computers. AT&T entered the show with all the 
resources you would expect from one   of the world's largest companies. Their 
exhibit was massive - someone mentioned   they had seen "entire shows conducted 
in smaller areas than AT&T's exhibit". They rented out the whole 31st floor 
of the Westin Bonaventure Hotel in   Los Angeles to bring together potential 
customers and an army of AT&T salespeople. At the show they presented the 3B 
series of minicomputers for business   accounting and office management. It 
included a single-user desktop 3B2,   the superminicomputers 3B5 and 3B20S, and the 
high-performance super-duper-minicomputer 3B20D. They all ran AT&T's self-made WE32000 CPU, 
256-kilobit memory, and ranged in price from   $10,000 for the low-end 3B2 to over $100,000 
for the 3B20S and $500,000 for the 3B20D. Reviewers liked the computers' 
obvious power - the WE32000 chip   was a beast. But they noted UNIX 
System V's complexity and lack of   user-friendliness compared to the Apple 
Macintosh OS, Lisa OS or even MS-DOS. For example, UNIX has 400 commands. Ordinary   users don't want to learn 400 
commands to use their computer. It seems weird to kick off with a bunch 
of computers that regular people can't   buy. But Jack Scanlon, president of AT&T's 
computer arm AT&T Information Systems, said: > "We know what we're doing in 
the computer business and I'm not   at all worried about us being 
able to take the next step." ## The Puzzling Model 6300 The 3B minicomputers were nice,   but people wanted to see AT&T battle 
IBM in the popular microcomputer sector. But here, they puzzled people 
with their next computer,   the Model 6300 - the outcome of its 
tieup with Olivetti. Reviewers were   disappointed to discover that the 6300 
was just another IBM PC running DOS. Released in late June 1984, it had a slightly 
faster Intel 8086 CPU and at $2,745 to   $4,920 was priced slightly lower 
than IBM's stuff, but that was it. This was weird. After all, didn't AT&T make a big   show of how they wanted to make UNIX 
an industry standard? That UNIX would   really tie all those computers together 
- just like that rug in the Big Lebowski? Charles Marshall, chairman of AT&T 
Information Systems, explained their thinking: > We had to recognize that in the marketplace 
today there are thousands of MS-DOS   machines ... Thousands of programs have been run 
under that system, and our customers have a big   investment in that software. For us to ignore that 
fact and go off on our own would not make sense. The 6300 can connect to the 3B UNIX 
minicomputers via Local Area Network   or LAN software. So the thinking was that 
users can run their existing DOS applications,   while also familiarizing themselves with 
UNIX through a communications terminal. AT&T managers also argued that marketing and 
selling the 6300 would help get people to see   this 99-year old company as doing 
computers and not just telephones. Not an unreasonable justification, but 
did they really have to put out such a   mid computer? It is interesting to note that 
the same week AT&T announced the Model 6300,   Compaq also announced their Deskpro, 
their first IBM-compatible desktop. The Deskpro remained compatible with 
DOS applications, but added new features   like additional slots for peripherals. 
Thusly differentiating itself from IBM's   products. Benjamin Rosen, Compaq's 
chairman told the New York Times: > There is this uninformed feeling in the industry 
that you can't conform with the I.B.M. standard   and differentiate your product at the same time. 
I think we are showing that this is not the case. ## A Bad Start International Data Corp estimated that 
in 1984, AT&T captured just 2.7% of   the medium-sized computer market. 
DEC led with 28.9% and IBM, 22.7%. Infocorp estimated that AT&T sold 
just 33,000 Model 6300s in 1984.   IBM, on the other hand, sold 
880,000 PCs that year. Even   Apple sold 275,000 Macintoshes. How 
sad is that? Even Apple did better! AT&T doesn't break out individual profit and 
loss figures in its official annual report,   but contemporary media estimated that their   computer and telephone equipment arm 
ATTIS lost about $750 million in 1983. In 1984, the company's full year 
profit of about $1.4 billion was   down substantially from expectations, due 
to product sales not being what they were. AT&T blamed this underperformance on 
several things. A worldwide shortage of   silicon in 1984 that hurt sales of larger systems. And there remained some residual regulatory 
limits that prevented AT&T from bundling   telephone and computer products together. 
Leading to a contradictory but rather amusing   situation where the AT&T Model 6300 computer 
cannot be sold in AT&T's own Phone Stores. So there was all that! But don't worry. Top 
management expected things to be better in 1985,   with AT&T even opening up sales of 
its own chips to other vendors. And   the aforementioned Charles Marshall said 
that their core industry focus was "small   business" and not the home market. So. No worries. ## The “Real” UNIX PC Even so, people still wanted to know: Where was 
the real AT&T PC? The one that would run UNIX?   This finally arrived in March 
1985 with the AT&T UNIX PC. Also called the Model 7300, the PC was built in 
conjunction with Convergent and priced at about   $5590. It had 512K of RAM, one floppy 
disk drive, and a 10 megabyte hard drive. The hardware has this slanted, 
distinct design that has shown   up in a few movies and TV shows in the late 1980s. And to smooth away UNIX's unfriendliness, AT&T 
layered a GUI on top of it. Users can navigate   menus and activate applications by clicking 
on them. Applications live inside windows   that you can resize, move around, and overlap 
with one another. There is also multi-tasking. Reviewers noted that the UNIX 
GUI - designed by a Princeton   professor named Carol Furchner - 
was not quite as polished as say,   the Macintosh's. It leans more on text than 
icons, which is what the Macintosh did. There were also some nagging issues.   The mouse pointer's accuracy was questionable. 
And the menu button placements lacked polish. Like a "Shut Down" command placed perilously 
close to the "Run" button. That is just evil. ## Bad Applications
However, reviewers universally said that the hardware was fine. The biggest 
problem were the applications. The UNIX PC's best software applications 
were - surprise - for communications.   You plugged your telephone into the computer, 
and then the computer to the wall jack. Then you can use the UNIX PC's software to 
automatically dial someone with a computerized   address book. It can record your calls and 
let you add little notes to those recordings.   And it even has a timer so you can manage your 
long-distance bill - wow forgot that existed. Beyond that, however, the application ecosystem 
was nothing like that of MS-DOS or even Apple.   AT&T bundled three applications for reviewers: 
A business graphics package, a word processor,   and a spreadsheet application 
called Supercomp-20 or now 20/20. Supercomp 20 worked, but not well. It 
doesn't work with the mouse and can't   handle a spreadsheet with 4,000 cells. 
And calculating a 3,000 cell sheet took   up to 11 minutes. Lotus 1-2-3 on an IBM 
PC on the other hand? Took just seconds. And the word processor was competent. It 
was modeled on Wang's Wangwriter - saying   that phrase was the only reason I 
added this section here - but ran   slow. It can't display more than 17 lines 
of 64 characters, which feels ... limiting. ## Where's the Beef?
We can blame some of these problems on not having enough memory. UNIX is said 
to be quite memory-hungry. But even if they added this expensive memory, 
the main issue is that UNIX was a ghost town,   applications-wise. I said before, in 1985 MS-DOS 
had five times more applications than UNIX did. For its UNIX PC, AT&T said that it would have 
28 applications at launch with "several more"   in the 90 days after. A few big names did 
agree to bring something to the market. Microsoft said it would “port” its word 
processor Word. Though that turned out a   version developed for their own UNIX 
variant XENIX and then translated to   the UNIX PC using an interpretation 
layer. So not a native experience. And Ashton-Tate, the famous software 
company, said it would port over its   popular database management software, 
dBASE. So in essence, dropping dBASE. But as for the third of the Big Three 
software companies in the 1980s, Lotus,   maker of the killer spreadsheet app 
Lotus-1-2-3. They still held out. The UNIX PC can technically 
run all UNIX-based software,   but reviewers noted that there were 
very few UNIX applications for small   businesses - even compared to CP/M, 
Tandy's TRDOS and even Apple's ProDOS. What happened to the partnership with the 
famous Digital Research Inc? The deal was   dissolved before the UNIX PC's release without 
much explanation and any tangible output. People   in the UNIX community thought the whole 
thing was vaporware from the beginning. The AT&T UNIX PC was literally made by 
a committee of marketers, scientists and   service personnel. The hardware boasted nothing 
exciting enough to get people to switch over. And as for UNIX, systems managers had long known 
of UNIX, but saw no reason to abandon the years   of training and software they had built up for 
IBM-associated operating systems to switch over   to it. Portability across machines and ideals 
like being “open” were for them not worth it. ## Falling Short and Backing Away Unit sales of the AT&T UNIX PC quickly slumped 
after its release. The only initial big buyers   were the Bell Operating Companies, AT&T's former 
subsidiaries, and those sales quickly petered out. In 1985, it was estimated that AT&T 
sold 12,000 to 18,000 UNIX PCs. IBM   sold a million IBM PCs. Apple sold 
420,000 Macs. Even the AT&T Model   6300 - that mid IBM-compatible - moved 
three times more units with 70,000. So AT&T’s next microcomputer 
was not another UNIX PC,   but the IBM compatible 6300 
Plus - released in October 1985. That was just an Olivetti M24, powered by the 
Intel 286, with some new software allowing it   to run both MS-DOS and UNIX applications side 
by side. Which was cool but still not enough. In mid-1986, Convergent Technologies, the OEM,   reported order cuts of UNIX 
PCs by AT&T due to poor sales. They received permission to 
try to sell the computer on   their own. Which they did, calling it the S/50. By late 1986, it was clear to outside 
observers that AT&T had lost the conviction   and determination it once had for the 
industry, especially microcomputers. They took just 6% of the market that year, 
almost all of it with IBM-compatible 6300s.   The microcomputer division was estimated 
to have lost an eye-popping $600 million   on $250-300 million of sales. Punishing 
layoffs were announced that year. Thomas Crotty of Gartner Securities 
said that AT&T was already out,   just maintaining their internal stuff: > They have $2 billion worth of their own systems   in house and will be spending time 
keeping those operations going. In October 1986, AT&T turned over 
their PC business to Olivetti and   halted shipments of the UNIX PC altogether. The reality was that the company had far bigger 
fish to fry back home in its core long-distance   business, which continued to face punishing, 
intense competition from MCI and Sprint. In 1988,   AT&T turned its first financial loss 
in 104 years, losing $1.67 billion. AT&T president Robert Allen 
said that in entering computers: > "Our appetite was too broad ... 
we learned a lot since then. Our   significant strength is in networking and 
we have a better sense of where we can play" Their failure in making and selling 
PC hardware would led them to strike   a deal with Sun, sparking the second 
phase of what we call the UNIX wars. On one positive note, they kept making their 
own minicomputers for a few more years. In 1988,   they introduced the super-mini 3B4000, 
known for its modular architecture. ## What Ifs Looking back, there are a 
few interesting what-ifs. What if the PC used the WE32000? You 
know, AT&T's own chip. The one it   made itself for its well-regarded 3B 
line. For reasons we may never know,   AT&T's bureaucracy prevented the company from 
releasing the chip's specs to Convergent. So Convergent built the UNIX PC with a 
Motorola 68010 CPU. A momentous decision   that cannot be reversed. Maybe the outcome 
would have been the same, but users of the   3B minicomputer line all said that thing 
screamed. Imagine all that power in a PC! What if they used their money to buy a 
distribution channel? Maybe the computer   retailer Radio Shack for direct access 
to the consumer. But I feel like such a   move would have probably alarmed 
their sales and retail partners. What if they truly open-sourced the 
UNIX code like how Google open-sourced   Android? AT&T did license the OS to 
Hewlett-Packard, DEC, Fujitsu and NEC. But licensees could not call it UNIX, and 
they often modified it into something weird.   I wonder if truly open-sourcing the 
code would have driven wider adoption,   attracted more application developers 
and truly leveraged UNIX’s portability. And what if AT&T ran the Compaq playbook? Though 
it didn't work out for them in the end, Compaq was   then in the midst of prying IBM's PC ecosystem 
away from it. The Model 6300 was a competent   computer. What if they just followed along in 
Compaq’s footsteps? Guess we will never know. ## Conclusion
All in all, AT&T seriously did the PC business for about a year. Maybe 2-3 at the 
most. Talk about "being in" right? In the end, the thing that most 
strikes me about AT&T's foray   into computers was its arrogance. 
A smugness that is hard to like. As they got started in 1984, AT&T ran 
an ad called the Computer Game. In it,   a person moves a small AT&T Model 6300 
board game piece alongside other computers,   and then moves it over a small bridge 
from MS-DOS into UNIX. The man moving the   piece then sits down with a smug smile and 
says "Your Move". What kind of ad is that? AT&T talked up their machines' technical 
quality and their ability to sell it to   Fortune 2000 companies and small businesses - with   their 6,000-strong sales force and bevy 
of corporate alliances. Against IBM! In 1985, when introducing 
the 6300 Plus, James Edwards,   AT&T Information Systems' president said: 
"We have out-PC-AT'ed IBM right now."   Quotes like these - and I mentioned a few more 
earlier in this video - just never look good. In the end, they couldn’t see what 
was in front of them. AT&T has a   reputation only a mother can love. 
Who ever has had a good interaction   with their telephone provider? Now 
imagine them providing your computer. American corporate history is littered 
with the corpses of big businesses that   tried to "do computer". AT&T - creator of 
the transistor, creator of UNIX - seemed   like it had a better chance than, say, 
Exxon. But they still failed all the same.

---
